title: Nadia's Orb-tastrophe
markdown:
Nadia the lynx kept the counter at The Bound Volumes the way some people keep secrets: wiped, aligned, unwilling to tolerate a spine out of true. The shop hummed with old paper. Knights and whispered spells stood in honest rows. A comma left in the wrong place, she was sure, could still unravel a kingdom, so she treated every shelf as a border that must not slip.

Every day the books clicked into place, a comfort as reliable as a clock.

Until one day a panicked flutter of feathers hit the doorway. The Great Bard’s Festival was in full swing. Tonight was the dress rehearsal of The Enigma of the Emerald Orb. The Orb — the star prop — was gone from its backstage pedestal. Not a missing trinket. A civic crisis in miniature.

Nadia’s mind ran like a catalogue. She would not merely report the gap. She would fill it. Mirrors, a discarded crystal chandelier, a luminous goose feather rescued from a forgotten epic: she would build a replacement that made audiences gasp.

Rafi the beaver, mentor of sturdy dams and sturdier advice, watched her scurry. “Nadia,” he rumbled, “are you sure? Sometimes the simplest solution is the strongest.”

She was sure. Her tail flicked double-time. Bartholomew the puffin, the playwright, wrung his wings in frantic circles. “The Emerald Orb must gleam with the light of a thousand forgotten stars.”

“It will,” Nadia said, and meant her contraption, and meant herself.

The stage washed in wavering light. The Orb pulsed, not with starlight but with the indecision of a faulty lamp. Actors tried to emote awe and achieved bewilderment. Professor Hoot, a stately owl, leaned toward his fellow. “Is it meant to be a disco ball,” he murmured, “or a particularly aggressive firefly?”

Nadia’s device was working beautifully, except that it looked nothing like an Emerald Orb. It looked like a startled pigeon in a lampshade.

A single snow-white feather, shed from Bartholomew’s wing, drifted from the rafters through the artificial glare and landed at the stage’s base, a quiet fact in a loud plan.

Rafi ambled on without mirrors. In his palm sat a small smooth green stone, cool, faintly mossy. “Bartholomew,” he said, “the light of a thousand forgotten stars is in the story, not the prop. A simple stone with a good tale may be enough.”

The owl nodded. The puffin blinked. Bartholomew looked from the flickering marvel to the stone, sighed the sigh of every misplaced prop in theatre history, and took the stone.

Actors gathered. The spotlight found green and earnest faces. Bartholomew began to speak of a mythical journey, and a gleam arrived that no feather or chandelier had managed: the warm kind, passed from mouth to ear.

Nadia felt her cleverness sit down. She had wanted to be the one who fixed everything with ingenuity. The show had needed a pebble and a sentence.

Ever since then she still alphabetizes The Bound Volumes until the spines click — and she leaves one extra space on the festival shelf, in case a story arrives that does not want arranging.
characters: Nadia (a lynx bookshop clerk), Rafi (a beaver mentor)
